_comment: Loco4CoCo arcade companion. Point at any account/event by editing this file only.

server._idle_shutdown_comment: 0 = never shut down, which is the right default for a booth. This was 45, and 45 minutes of quiet at a stand is an ordinary lunchtime - the failure mode was a dead stand when the next visitor walked up, with nobody watching the terminal to notice. Cost is not a reason to keep it: the warehouse auto-suspends on its own (auto_suspend was raised to 3600s on 2026-09-22 so the visitor never pays a ~56s cold start), and the booth warehouse measured 0.78 credits in 14 days. Set a number of minutes if you specifically want an unattended laptop to stop itself.

event._event_name_comment: What visitors see as the event: the docx 'Prepared for ... - <event_name>.' line, the share card and CoCo's persona. Independent of venue (which only picks datasets and region). Empty falls back to 'Snowflake World Tour <city>'.
event._venue_comment: The ONE toggle a booth operator changes per event. Expands via the venues map below into city, language, cloud region and marketplace profile. One of: london, paris, berlin (the three SWT events) or tel_aviv (Hayadata) - and ONLY those. This comment used to list frankfurt as a fourth, which is wrong and was actively dangerous: Frankfurt is the ACCOUNT's region, not an event, and resolve_venue() answers an unknown venue by quietly defaulting market_profile to 'uk', so an operator who trusted this line and set venue to 'frankfurt' would have stood up a booth serving London's datasets with no error anywhere. Do not add a venue here without adding it to the venues map, and do not add one that is not an event. Leave unset to hand-configure city/language/region directly.
event._marketplace_region_comment: The EVENT's region - where the visitors live. Used ONLY to decide which Marketplace datasets are PREFERRED in the recommendations. Resolved from event.venue; you do not set it by hand. It is NOT the account's region and must never be confused with it: the account's region only decides where SESSIONS/TURNS/blueprints are written, is whatever the DataOps pool assigned, and is never needed. Renamed from `region`, which did not say which of the two it meant. Offering a visitor a share they cannot attach wastes the five minutes we just spent with them.
event.title: Loco for CoCo
event.subtitle: Five minutes to your next data product
event._byline_comment: Shown under the title on the start screen. Left EMPTY by default so a fresh cloner does not ship someone else's name at their own event. Set it to your own, or leave blank to show nothing.
event._attribution_comment: There is deliberately no operator/stand field. It was a hand-typed label that no logic read, and every row written before it was removed had it empty. The question it was for - which laptop produced this row - is already answered by the account, because a second laptop at an event is given its own pool account. SESSIONS.SE_OPERATOR is now stamped with CURRENT_ACCOUNT() automatically.

venues._comment: The three SWT events plus Hayadata (tel_aviv). event.venue selects one; resolve_venue() in server.py overwrites event.city/language/marketplace_region and sets event.market_profile from it. TWO REGIONS EXIST AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME THING. (1) `marketplace_region` below is the EVENT LOCATION's cloud region and is used ONLY to judge which Marketplace datasets to RECOMMEND - London prioritises AWS_EU_WEST_2 listings, Paris AWS_EU_WEST_3, Berlin AWS_EU_CENTRAL_1. (2) The ACCOUNT's own region is whatever the DataOps pool assigns (register once per event at https://go.dataops.live/emea-swt/register; the account name is random and its region is not guaranteed) and is used ONLY for where SESSIONS/TURNS/blueprints are written - it must NEVER filter recommendations. Nothing in the setup asks the operator for the account's name or region, which is precisely why a random pool assignment is safe. The visitor never imports anything at the booth: they leave with links and open them later from their own account, so what matters is that a dataset is relevant and available WHERE THEY ARE, not whether the booth could attach it. Because one account serves one event, LOCO4COCO.BOOTH is the per-event separation and there are deliberately no per-event schemas. NOTE: only the 'en' UI copy deck exists; fr/de language codes are wired but the copy is still English (translation deprioritised).
venues._tel_aviv_comment: Hayadata, Tel Aviv. Snowflake has no Israel region, so recommendations are judged against AWS Frankfurt (eu-central-1), where Israeli accounts most often sit. The il profile is global datasets that cover Israel: almost nothing on the Marketplace is Israel-specific, and the one listing that is (OpenStreetMap Israel) is by-request. Curated 2026-10-15.

snowflake._connection_name_comment: Placeholder. bootstrap.py sets this to YOUR snow connection (step_config). It is the connection the postbox uses for `snow stage copy` and GET_PRESIGNED_URL, so a stale or someone-else's value here is the classic postbox failure. Never commit a real connection name: the repo ships MYBOOTH on purpose and scripts/check_config_portable.py enforces it.
snowflake._snow_binary_comment: Path to the Snowflake CLI. Same idea as coco.binary: pip installs snow into the Python bin/ directory, which is often not on the default macOS PATH. If 'snow' is not found at startup, the banner says so and names the fix. Set an absolute path here if the binary is installed but not on PATH.

coco._comment: Each message spawns `cortex exec`. Deliberately UNCAPPED - no max-turns, no effort floor, history left on. Cost is managed by observation (see cost_log) not by throttling the visitor.
coco._model_comment: AGENT model, for `cortex exec` and `cortex mcp serve` (the Workshop). This is the Cortex Code namespace - the names in the Cortex Code model picker: claude-opus-5, claude-sonnet-5, openai-gpt-5.4, grok-4.6. It is NOT the same namespace as complete_model below, and mixing them up fails: `mistral-large2` and `llama3.1-70b` are valid for COMPLETE but rejected by `cortex exec`, and `gemini-flash-3.7` appears in the picker but works in neither on an event account. null means let Cortex Code choose (Auto), which is the safest default because it survives a model being retired.
coco._complete_model_namespace: SQL model, for SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX.COMPLETE (the Library, Marketplace and Postbox reflections, and QA). Do NOT put a coco.model value here without checking it, and do not put one of these in coco.model. The two namespaces OVERLAP but are not equal - measured on an AWS eu-central-1 event account: claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5, openai-gpt-5.4 and grok-4.6 work in BOTH; openai-gpt-5, openai-gpt-5-mini and llama3.1-70b work in COMPLETE ONLY; mistral-large2 is legacy in COMPLETE and rejected by cortex exec; gemini-flash-3.7 works in neither. Verify with scripts/rebench_complete.py, which tests COMPLETE specifically.
coco.complete_model_fallbacks_comment: Tried in order at server start if complete_model does not answer. This exists because claude-4-sonnet went to legacy state mid-project and every COMPLETE turn failed silently for a whole test run while the slow exec fallback covered for it. A model name is a perishable dependency, so the booth now proves it at startup rather than discovering it in front of a visitor.
coco.warm_agent_comment: Hold a `cortex mcp serve` process open between visitors. Measured ~3.9s per turn against ~22s for a cold `cortex exec`, because exec has no --resume/--session and pays ~18s of process startup every call. Strictly one in-flight call: concurrent calls on one process were proven to mis-correlate and return another call’s answer. SAFE TO LEAVE TRUE ON ANY LAPTOP: `cortex mcp serve` is not a stable contract across versions, so all four ways it can fail (binary absent, exits at once, serves without a cortex_code_agent tool, or serves and never replies) were tested with stub binaries and each now degrades in bounded time to `cortex exec`. A version with no cortex_code_agent is detected once at startup and logged, not rediscovered every turn. Set false only to force the exec path for comparison.
coco.turn_timeout_comment: Wall-clock ceiling per turn, for the FAST stops. The Library has been measured at a 127.3s outlier against a 2.2s median; past the ceiling the visitor is better served by the precomputed answer than a better sentence. LOWERED 60 -> 30 on 2026-09-22 after grepping every timeout in the booth: with the warehouse held warm (auto_suspend 3600) a proven COMPLETE turn is 1.4-2.1s, so 60s was ~30x the measured worst case and could only ever be reached by a pathology - and when it was reached, a visitor stood in front of a frozen screen for a full minute with a queue behind them. 30s and NOT tighter, deliberately: a visitor who writes a long, complex brief earns a slower answer, and capping them out for being thorough would punish exactly the engagement this booth exists to provoke. So this is a floor under the worst case, not a target - roughly 14x the median, with the precomputed archetype content waiting on the other side of it. The Workshop overrides this (locations.workshop.timeout) because it is the one agentic turn and legitimately takes 20-27s.
coco._complete_model_comment: RE-MEASURED 2026-09-21 on an AWS eu-central-1 event account after the previous default BROKE. claude-4-sonnet went to legacy state and now returns a 400 in ~0.5s on every call ('The model claude-4-sonnet has been in legacy state'), so every COMPLETE turn was failing and the 20-27s cortex exec fallback was silently carrying the load. mistral-large2 is ALSO legacy now, and the entire Claude family (claude-4-5-sonnet, claude-3-5-sonnet, claude-4-opus) plus openai-gpt-4.1-mini and snowflake-llama-3.3-70b are unknown/unavailable here. Survivors, 2 reps on the Dynamic Tables quality probe: openai-gpt-5 1.6s and CORRECT; openai-gpt-5-mini 2.3s but recommended Streams and Tasks; llama3.1-70b 1.4s but recommended Materialized Views; llama3.3-70b 45.8s and also wrong. openai-gpt-5 is the only model that is both fast and right, so it is the default for replies and for QA. MODEL AVAILABILITY MOVES UNDER YOU: run scripts/rebench_complete.py against the event account before every event, and check /admin shows a reply model that actually answers.
coco._complete_model_fallbacks_comment: Tried in order when the primary is dead. All three verified in AWS_EU_CENTRAL_1 at 1.4-2.0s by scripts/audit_ai_paths.py. grok-4.6 was removed: it answers correctly but latency measured 2.7/48/53/77s, and a 50s median is worse than simply falling through to cortex exec at ~23s, so as a fallback it made things slower rather than safer.
coco.binary_comment: Path to the Cortex Code CLI. Honoured by the exec path, the marketplace search AND the warm agent - agent_pool used to hardcode \cortex\, so setting an absolute path here once gave a working exec beside a warm agent that silently never started.

qa._comment: The QA bot reviews the finished blueprint before it is staged. Deterministic checks always run and silently repair what is fixable from the closed lists (off-list features dropped, guide fallback, platforms re-normalised); each change is recorded to LOCO4COCO.BOOTH.QA_FINDINGS with before/after, and a summary lands on the SESSIONS row. model_review adds one fast COMPLETE call judging whether the POC addresses the visitor's stated problem - it fails open, never blocking the handover.

delivery._comment: Delivery is a QR code pointing at the visitor's .docx, staged and presigned on @LOCO4COCO.BOOTH.BLUEPRINTS (presign_seconds = 7 days). There is deliberately no email and no local record: email was removed (snowflake.com publishes DMARC p=reject, and the Gmail MCP cannot send or attach under `cortex exec`), so the old outbox that wrote visitor PII to disk on every visit was pure liability on a shared laptop and is gone. The governed Snowflake SESSIONS row is the only kept record of a visitor.

intake._comment: CoCo gets up and asks who the present is for. Typing is limited to these three fields plus any 'Other' answers.
intake.industry_question: And what world do you work in? I'll fill the library with the right shelves.
intake.confirm_industry: I'm guessing {industry} from {company} - have I got that right?

letter._comment: The opening is a sequence, not a form: CoCo is home, a letter arrives, and the letter itself IS the intake. Every phase is click-skippable so a booth operator is never trapped in an animation.
letter.arctic_sub: (Yes, penguins live in Antarctica, but CoCo is special!)
body: I've heard you and the Cortex Crew have been cooking up some amazing products recently.
Me and my team at {company} wanted to learn more.
We're particularly interested in {industry} and wanted to understand what a Proof of Concept (POC) would look like for this on Snowflake.
letter.line1: A letter, from my friend {first_name}! Better get to work...
letter.line2: Anyway, let's go and get this show on the road.
letter.map_line: First stop is my Data Library. That's where I keep all the unstructured, semi-structured and structured data that would be useful for {first_name} and {company}.
letter.bubble:
Wow, a letter from my friend! Shame I can't make out some of these words...
(Please fill this in with your details)

intake.problem_label: The problem you want to solve (two sentences)
intake.problem_placeholder: e.g. our engineers waste hours hunting through old inspection reports. We want answers in seconds, with the source.
intake._problem_placeholder_comment: intake.problem_placeholder is the fallback shown before an industry is chosen. Once one is picked, industries.<key>.problem_placeholder replaces it so the example belongs to the visitor's world.

healthcare.name: Healthcare & Life Sciences

data_sources.label: Patient records
data_sources.note: Structured clinical records in a PAS or EPR system

data_sources.label: Clinical notes & letters
data_sources.note: Free text - discharge summaries, referrals, correspondence

healthcare.problem_placeholder: e.g. our clinicians re-read discharge summaries to find one detail. We want the answer in seconds, with the source.

financial.name: Financial Services

data_sources.label: Regulatory reporting
data_sources.note: Submissions and the reconciliations behind them

financial.problem_placeholder: e.g. every complaint is read by hand to spot the urgent ones. We want them sorted and routed the moment they land.

retail.name: Retail & Consumer Goods

data_sources.label: Sales & till transactions
data_sources.note: Basket-level sales by store and channel

data_sources.label: Supplier & logistics data
data_sources.note: Purchase orders, lead times, delivery performance

data_sources.label: Reviews & customer service
data_sources.note: Free text feedback, returns reasons, contact logs

retail.problem_placeholder: e.g. nobody can say why a line sold out in one region and sat still in another. We want that answered without a data team.

public.name: Public Sector & Government

data_sources.label: Policy & guidance documents
data_sources.note: Years of PDFs, circulars and statutory guidance

public.problem_placeholder: e.g. our guidance sits in years of PDFs nobody can search. We want caseworkers to ask a question and get a cited answer.

manufacturing.name: Manufacturing & Industrial

data_sources.label: Machine & sensor telemetry
data_sources.note: High frequency readings off the line

data_sources.label: Maintenance logs
data_sources.note: Work orders and engineer free text

data_sources.label: Supplier & inbound logistics
data_sources.note: Component lead times and quality by supplier

data_sources.label: Energy consumption
data_sources.note: Meter data by line and site

manufacturing.problem_placeholder: e.g. we find out a machine was failing after it stopped. We want the warning while there is still time to act.

energy.name: Energy & Utilities

data_sources.label: Field engineer reports
data_sources.note: Free text inspection and repair notes

energy.problem_placeholder: e.g. engineer notes and meter data live apart, so we cannot connect a fault to what led to it. We want them joined up.

media.name: Media, Telco & Entertainment

data_sources.label: Viewing & listening events
data_sources.note: Play, pause, completion by title and device

media.problem_placeholder: e.g. we know what was watched but not why anyone churned. We want the two joined so we can see it coming.

other.name: Something else

data_sources.label: Core operational records
data_sources.note: Whatever your main system of record holds

data_sources.label: Documents & PDFs
data_sources.note: Years of unstructured files nobody can query

data_sources.label: Customer or member data
data_sources.note: Who you serve and what they have done

other.problem_placeholder: e.g. the answer exists somewhere in our systems and it takes days to get it out. We want it in seconds, with the source.

library.name: The Data Library
library.heading: Which of these do you work with at the moment?
library.hint: Tick everything that applies. Add your own if it's missing.
library.narrative: This is my magic data library, {first_name}. Every shelf can mimic something {company} already holds. You can ask me for anything, from MP3 to CSV, PDF to Parquet.
library.prompt:
The visitor works in {industry} at {company}. They described their problem as: "{problem}". In THE LIBRARY they said they already hold: {selection}, sitting on {platforms}. Reply in at most 2 short sentences: connect the most valuable thing in that list to the problem they described, and name ONE specific, named Snowflake feature that would unlock it (for example Cortex Analyst, Cortex Search, Snowpark, Dynamic Tables, ML Classification, Snowflake Marketplace). Name the feature, not a general ability like handling large datasets. Warm, plain English, no jargon, no bullet points, no headings, no em dashes.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.

marketplace.name: The Marketplace
marketplace.heading: What shall we join to your data?
marketplace.hint: Live listings, filtered to what you can attach in this region. No ETL, no storage cost, refreshed by the provider. The same door works outwards: this is how you share your own data without handing over a copy.
marketplace.other_placeholder: e.g. Israeli address data, company registry data
marketplace._discovery_comment: manual = serve the CURATED marketplace-index.md, which is what the offline agentic-search precompute produced: 6 verified, free, UK-weighted, importability-checked picks per industry. This is deliberate for a branded event. MEASURED with discovery='live': public sector returned three Met Office weather products plus 'India Economic Monitor', because live matching ranked raw keyword hits with no geography and pinned two weather listings; after adding geo weighting and per-industry avoid terms it returned only 4 results, two of them weak ('UN Codes for Trade and Transport', 'Overture Maps'). Curation beats liveness on a stand: the stall must be predictable and defensible. Set to 'live' to use SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS (region + is_ready_for_import + geo weighting + industry_avoid), falling back here below min_live_results.
marketplace.narrative: This is the Snowflake Marketplace, and every stall is a real company's data. You attach it and query it live, seconds later. You never copy it, you never build a pipeline for it, and you never pay to store it.
marketplace.prompt:
The visitor's stated problem is: "{problem}". Keep your answer pointed at it.
The visitor works in {industry} at {company} and holds: {held}. In THE MARKETPLACE they chose to join these real Snowflake Marketplace listings: {selection}. Reply in at most 2 short sentences: say what joining those lets them answer that they cannot answer today. Refer to the datasets only by the names given above; do not invent any other listing or provider name. Plain English, no bullet points, no em dashes.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.

workshop._background_comment: Run the workshop draft in the background: CoCo answers at once with background_ack, the postbox unlocks, and the agent (10-40s) drafts while the visitor walks. The real reply lands in the bubble when ready; the postbox shows finishing until then. Set false to hold the visitor at the bench as before.
workshop.background_ack: Brilliant - I am sketching your proof of concept now. Head to the postbox and grab any bonuses on the way, I will tell you what I came up with as you walk.
workshop.background_ready: Your blueprint is ready at the postbox.
workshop.postbox_ready_nudge: Your blueprint is ready - head to the postbox!
workshop.locked_pending: CoCo is already drafting your blueprint - head to the postbox.
workshop.locked_done: Your blueprint is waiting for you at the postbox.
workshop.name: The Workshop
workshop.heading: What do we want our Proof of Concept to do?
workshop.hint: Think big and say it in one line. An AI agent that answers for you, a dashboard that explains itself, an app your team actually opens every morning, something that spots trouble before it lands. Whatever it is, we forge it here.
workshop.placeholder: e.g. an agent that answers policy questions with citations
workshop.narrative: Bench cleared, forge lit. Tell me what the finished thing does and I'll draw up the plan.
workshop.prompt:
The visitor's stated problem is: "{problem}". Keep your answer pointed at it.
The visitor is {first_name}, {industry}, at {company}. They hold: {held}. They will join: {joined}. In THE WORKSHOP they said the POC should: "{input}".

On the way here they also answered these bonus questions. Treat them as facts about their situation and let them decide the archetype, the name and the features where they apply:
{bonus}

First choose the archetype that matches what they are ACTUALLY trying to do. Pick exactly one of these keys:
talk-to-my-data (ask questions of structured data in plain English)
ask-my-documents (search or Q&A over documents and free text)
extract-from-paperwork (pull structured fields out of forms, invoices, letters)
triage-and-classify (sort, route or prioritise incoming items)
an-agent-that-acts (takes an action, not just answers)
predict-what-happens-next (forecasting or risk scoring)
join-the-silos (unify data that lives in separate systems)
share-without-copying (give someone else live access)
watch-it-live (streaming or near real-time monitoring)

The data they hold decides this. If their source is documents or free text, it is ask-my-documents or extract-from-paperwork, NOT talk-to-my-data.

For features, you MUST choose 2 to 4 names EXACTLY as spelled from this list and nothing else:
{feature_list}

Return ONLY minified JSON, no prose and no code fence, with exactly these keys:
{"archetype": one key from the list above, "poc_name": short name in their own language, max 8 words, "features": array of 2-4 names copied exactly from the feature list, "reply": max 40 words, warm, spoken aloud to them, and if they answered any bonus questions mention one of their answers naturally so they hear it was used, no bullet points, no em dashes}

Nothing else is wanted. Do NOT write a summary, considerations, a first step or a score - those are filled in elsewhere, and every extra word here is time the visitor spends waiting at the bench. Never claim the POC is built.

Word choice matters: this goes into a document handed to a visitor at a public booth. Never use the words die, dies, dying, kill, killed, killing, suicide, cripple or crippled, and never use violent or morbid metaphors for systems failing. Say fails, stops, degrades or goes down instead. Keep the register plain and calm.
workshop._timeout_comment: The ONE stop that overrides coco.turn_timeout, and it overrides it upwards. This is the only agentic turn (transport exec, tools on, max_turns 4) and has been measured at 20-27s, so the tight global ceiling would cut it off mid-think and hand back precomputed content on the single beat of the visit where the bespoke answer is the whole point. 60s is roughly twice the measured worst case. It stays a ceiling, not a licence: past it the fallback still carries the visit rather than leaving the bench hanging.
workshop._tool_hint_comment: Set to e.g. 'Use your tools to check the Snowflake docs before choosing features.' to make the tray show real tool calls. Measured cost: about 34s for one lookup, so it is off by default. The Ask stop is the budgeted place for tool use.

postbox.name: The Postbox
postbox.heading: Shall I post it?
postbox.hint: I'll write it up properly and put it in the post.
postbox.narrative: Wrapped, labelled and ready. Say the word and I'll put it in your hands.
postbox._button_comment: Two presses, two labels. The first press MAKES the thing, so it says so; the second press comes after the QR code is on screen, when the document already exists and all that is left is to watch it arrive. Both were 'POST IT TO ME', which read as if the first press had not worked.

intro.title: Loco for CoCo
body: This is a fun way to experience the power of Cortex Code (CoCo) through the medium of an arcade game.

You have 5 minutes to explore what building a Proof of Concept on Snowflake really looks like, with CoCo as your guide to our features, marketplace datasets, and how enterprise-grade AI can bring your ideas to life.
You will leave with a personalised action plan for building it for real. Be daring, this is a flexible process with a genuinely useful outcome.
*Anything you type stays private*, only shared with you and Snowflake.

ask._comment: The one unscripted stop. Always exec (never the fast path): this is where real CoCo earns it, because nothing is injected for it to reflect back, so it has a genuine reason to use its tools. Optional and skippable so it cannot blow the five minutes.
ask.heading: Ask CoCo one thing
ask.hint: Optional. One question about your POC and CoCo will look it up properly.
ask.placeholder: e.g. what would we need before we could trust the predictions?
ask.tool_hint: Use your tools to check the Snowflake documentation before you answer, so the answer is grounded rather than guessed. One lookup is enough.
ask._status: Disabled: it must be a deliberate beat in the flow, not a popup. The /api/ask endpoint and the card are built and proven (real tool call, grounded answer) - re-enable when it has its own step or tile.

bonus._comment: Optional bonus objectives on the map. Never interrupts the main flow: an object spawns only while the visitor is walking (no interior or overlay open), with a countdown to REACH it, no timer to answer. Questions are generated by COMPLETE in the background from everything known so far; if generation fails nothing spawns. Missed ones can be answered at the postbox for half points. Answers feed the POC, the kickoff prompt, the docx and SESSIONS.BONUS_QA. The score is computed server-side only; the scoreboard reads SESSIONS (this account, today) so nothing is kept on the laptop.

scoring._comment: map is the MINIMUM for a bonus answered on the map; it is multiplied by up to map_max_multiplier the faster the visitor reaches it (full multiplier at spawn, falling linearly to x1 when the countdown ends). postbox is the flat half-points catch-up.

bonus.prompt:
You are helping shape a Snowflake proof of concept for a booth visitor. Here is everything we know so far:
{known}

Ask the ONE short question whose answer would most change or sharpen this proof of concept, that we do not already know. It must be answerable by tapping one of 2 to 4 short options. Plain everyday language a business person understands: no jargon, no product or feature names, never mention Snowflake or AI. Never ask for names, emails, phone numbers or any personal or contact details. Each question must cover a DIFFERENT decision topic from every topic already covered. Two questions are the same topic if their answers would tell us the same thing, even when the wording differs (for example 'which goal matters most' and 'what would make this most valuable first' are the same topic: the first business goal). Good distinct topics include: the first business goal, who uses the result, how fresh the data must be, how much data, the main blocker, whether personal data is involved, when success should show, who signs it off - but choose whatever matters most for THIS visitor.

Reply with minified JSON only, no prose: {"topic": "2 to 4 word name of the decision topic", "question": "...", "options": ["...", "..."], "why": "one short internal reason"}. Question at most 90 characters, each option at most 32 characters.

copy.card_hint: Tap an answer - CoCo will use it in your blueprint.
copy._other_comment: Every bonus question also offers a free-text answer. The server accepts it only under this exact label, trims it to other_max chars and refuses anything that looks like an email or phone number.
copy.missed_toast: Missed it - you can still answer at the postbox for half points.
copy.missed_hint: Optional, half points each. CoCo will add them to your blueprint.
copy.brief_prefix: Keep in mind what I told you:

qualification._comment: SE scoring. Three 1-5 scores decide whether the use case is worth an SE's time: NOW (the visitor's own capacity answer at the postbox, scored from the option below), SOLVABLE and CONSUMPTION (one COMPLETE call against the rubric in the prompt). Average >= pass_threshold qualifies: the visitor gets the blueprint and is told they can talk to an SE. Below it, the game ends with a friendly message and no blueprint. The scores themselves go ONLY to SESSIONS.SE_* and are stripped from every endpoint the browser reads. If the model call fails, SOLVABLE and CONSUMPTION default to fallback_score so a Snowflake outage never turns a visitor away.

capacity.heading: One last thing: when could your team start on this?
capacity.hint: Be honest - it only decides what happens next.
capacity.required: Pick one so CoCo knows what happens next.

qualification.qualified_line: Good news, {first_name}: this use case qualifies for a conversation with a Snowflake SE. Grab one at the stand and show them your blueprint.
qualification.not_qualified_body: From what you told me, this one is better as an idea to come back to than a project to start today. Keep thinking about it - when the timing and the data line up, Snowflake will be here, and so will I.
qualification.not_qualified_reply: Thanks, {first_name} - from what you told me, this one is better as an idea to come back to than a project to start today. When the timing and the data line up, come and find us.

marketplace._comment: Live discovery needs NO private preview: SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS piped through RESULT_SCAN gives 188 importable listings in AWS_EU_WEST_2 (of 4327 total, 799 region-available). Measured 2026-08-17. The curated index stays as the offline-safe fallback.
marketplace._locality_comment: market_profile -> the country the agentic search should prefer. This is what makes the 7th 'something else' option local to the EVENT rather than to the account: every event account is in AWS Frankfurt, so the region is a constraint on what can be attached, while the country below is what makes a suggestion relevant. Proven: asking for Germany returned GfK Population Germany and Acxiom EMEA Geo-Spatial DE.

agentic._comment: THE 7th OPTION. Triggered ONLY when a visitor TYPES into the marketplace 'something else' box. Uses `cortex search marketplace` with a cloudRegion filter taken from event.marketplace_region (the EVENT’s region, resolved from event.venue) - NOT a free-form agent prompt. MEASURED: the prompt route took 110-237s and returned out-of-region results 78 times out of 91; the filtered search takes 6.8-8.3s and is in-region by construction, with provider names included. All three event regions were verified answering from one AWS Frankfurt account, because the Marketplace catalogue is global. Still fired in the BACKGROUND and merged into the takeaway document at the postbox, so a slow call can never hold up the stall. The six curated picks stay deterministic and are never waited on. Watch cost.jsonl (kind=marketplace_agentic).

marketplace._pinned_comment: Verified importable in AWS_EU_WEST_2 on 2026-08-17. Met Office profile GZTDZJKVBD. Surfaced first when the live tier finds them. Ordnance Survey is deliberately absent: it is NOT on the Marketplace in any region, so it lives in config.sourcing instead.

provider_names._comment: SHOW AVAILABLE LISTINGS returns an opaque profile id, not a display name.

marketplace._exclude_comment: Keyword matching pulls in tools and apps, not just data. A healthcare stall offering 'Snowflake Health Check Dashboard' reads as broken, so obvious non-dataset titles are dropped.
marketplace._geo_comment: The event is a UK stand, so a UK visitor must not be offered 'India Economic Monitor' or 'All International Postal Codes' ahead of the ONS census. `prefer` terms score a listing UP, `demote` terms score it DOWN, and keyword matches are ranked by that score instead of catalogue order. Change these when the event moves country - nothing here is hardcoded.
marketplace._avoid_comment: Per-industry veto. The public-sector keyword 'postcode' was matching 'Postcode Sector Weather Forecasts' - a weather product - so three of the six public-sector picks were Met Office. These terms drop a listing from an industry even when a keyword hit.

il._comment: Israel-specific listings barely exist, so global and multi-country data is PREFERRED here, not demoted as it is for the European profiles. Only single-country content from elsewhere is pushed down.

geo_by_profile._comment: Per market_profile geo weighting for the live/agentic tiers. uk falls back to the 'geo' block above. prefer scores a listing up, demote scores it down. The manual/curated stall does not use geo - its localisation is which listings are curated per profile plus the region filter.

marketplace._themes_comment: What a listing is FOR, and what a shelf in the library IS. Selection intersects the two, so a visitor who ticked "clinical notes" is offered document-shaped joins and one who ticked "estates and operations" is offered geography and telemetry. Tagging 30 listings does the work that industry x archetype curation would need 72 hand-written lists to do, and it keeps every offered row a real, importability-checked listing.
marketplace._documents_gap_comment: There is deliberately no "documents" theme. The curated set contains no listing that helps a visitor whose problem is unstructured text: PubMed and the social-conversations sample are reference corpora, not document-processing enablers, and tagging them that way surfaced biomedical papers to a council holding policy PDFs. This is a real gap in the curated set, recorded rather than papered over with a mis-tag.
marketplace._bucket_only_comment: Listings that must never be borrowed into another industry, KEYED BY MARKET PROFILE. Cross-bucket borrowing is right for data that travels - weather, boundaries, addresses, population, company registrations, industry classifications - and wrong for sector-specific reference and market data: scoring alone once offered PubMed biomedical papers to a council holding policy PDFs, because both matched on 'population'. THIS USED TO BE A FLAT LIST and therefore only protected the profile it was written for: 12 of 12 entries were London listings, so Paris and Berlin had NO protection at all and a French health-insurance corpus could be borrowed into a manufacturing stall. It cannot be derived from the data - 37 London listings sit in exactly one industry and only 11 are protected - so it is a curation judgement and each profile needs its own entries. A flat list is still honoured, and is treated as uk.

sourcing._comment: Where data can come from when the visitor is NOT yet a Snowflake customer. Ordnance Survey lives here rather than in the Marketplace because it is not listed there in any region (checked 2026-08-17); Open UPRN exists but is not available in AWS_EU_WEST_2.
sourcing.synthetic_hint: CoCo can mimic any shelf as synthetic data so a POC can start before the real feed exists. Generate it in Snowflake with GENERATOR and RANDOM, or let Cortex fabricate realistic rows from a description.

platforms._comment: Where the data lives today. Asked on CoCo's home stage (moved out of the library 2026-08-25), one tap; decides the integration-path section of the blueprint.
platforms.heading: We currently keep data on…
platforms.hint: Tap every platform it sits on. This is what decides how we get it into Snowflake.
platforms._guardrail: `exclusive` chips cannot be combined with a named source: "Already in Snowflake" prints "nothing to move" and "Not sure yet" prints "go and ask", so pairing either with Oracle or AWS made the blueprint contradict itself. The UI clears the other group on tap and the server re-normalises, so a bypassed UI cannot produce a contradictory document. `max_routes` caps the ingestion section: 8 chips printed 8 route paragraphs and 5 Openflow mentions, which read as a template rather than a plan.
platforms._exclusive_comment: Only "Not sure yet" is exclusive, because it is the absence of an answer rather than an answer. "Already in Snowflake" is deliberately NOT exclusive: an organisation can have data in Snowflake AND in Oracle, and forcing a choice made the visitor misrepresent their estate. When it is combined with a named source the blueprint prints a combined route (see PLATFORM_COMBINED in server.py) rather than "nothing to move".

country._comment: Home-stage question 2. Europe-weighted for London/Paris. Frames the residency follow-up.
country.heading: As you'll remember CoCo, we're based in
country.hint: Tap every country you have a base in. It helps me keep your data where your rules need it.
country._default_comment: When set to one of the options, the letter does not ask where the visitor is based: the question is hidden and this answer is recorded. Hayadata is a Tel Aviv event, so Israel. Empty string asks the question again.

residency._comment: The residency question is no longer asked. It is inferred from the location given on the letter: one country means that country, several mean the EU, anywhere outside means no assumption. These values still reach the blueprint and the SESSIONS row; only the question is gone. fallback_country names a country when none was given.
residency._eu_countries_comment: Several countries are read as 'must stay in the EU' ONLY when every one picked is listed here. Israel + United States is not an EU constraint.
residency._region_names_comment: How a country reads as the place data stays. Israel has no Snowflake region, so the blueprint must NOT promise data stays in Israel; it says the visitor's chosen region instead.

sovereignty._comment: Visitor-facing sovereignty copy. react.* are CoCo's one-liners on the home stage, keyed by the answer. pillars.* are reused verbatim in the blueprint's Sovereignty & security section. Kept here so Paris is a copy swap.

react.platform_already: Perfect - it's already in Snowflake, so we skip the plumbing and go straight to building.
react.platform_unsure: No problem - we'll work the plumbing out together, it's usually the easy part.
react.platform_named: Good - I know exactly how to get data out of {platform} and into Snowflake, in region and without copying it around.
react.country: {country}, lovely. I'll keep everything where {country}'s rules need it.

pillars.data: By default your data does not leave {region}: it stays in your own Snowflake account, in region, not copied out to be processed.
pillars.models: By default, Cortex runs the AI models in your own region, so nothing has to cross a border to be understood.
pillars.marketplace: Marketplace data is shared live rather than copied, and you are only ever offered listings available in {region}.
pillars.governance: One set of controls - role-based access, masking, row-level policies - governs all of it, in one place.

sovereignty._summary_comment: Spoken over the house scene after the letter is submitted. CoCo reads back what was given, then makes the security and AI point inside that summary rather than as a separate beat. Placeholders: {first_name}, {company_bit}, {industry_bit}, {platform_bit}, {region}. The _bit placeholders are assembled by the client from what the visitor actually supplied, so a missing answer leaves no dangling sentence. Each line auto-advances on a timer scaled to its length.
summary: So, {first_name}, let me make sure I have this. {company_bit}{industry_bit}{platform_bit}I have the problem you want to solve, and that is the bit everything else hangs off.

Here is the part that matters before we start building. By default, all of this happens inside your own Snowflake account in {region}. Your data does not get copied out to be processed, and the AI models run in your own region, so nothing has to cross a border to be understood.

Snowflake never uses your Customer Data to train models made available to our customer base. Your data is not available to other customers or model developers. And you have control over your team's use of Snowflake AI Features through familiar role-based access control.
You will not have to move house for any of it either. Snowflake talks to what you already run, and with Iceberg your tables stay in open formats other engines can read, so there is no one way door.

screens._comment: Visitor-facing prose that belongs to a screen rather than to a stop. It lived in index.html, which meant it never appeared in the "every scripted line" section of the decision tree, so the document claimed a completeness it did not have. Anything a visitor reads belongs here.
